title: King Lear
wpTitle: King Lear starring Kenneth Branagh – Reviews

ratings.excerpt: Kenneth Branagh’s fast and feverish tragedy … At two hours with no interval, the actor-director’s production hurtles past at such speed that the depths of the play are too rarely realised … We have come to expect great things: energy, polish and accomplished verse diction. That is what we get here, in his production of what some believe to be the most tragic of Shakespearean downfalls. But although Branagh delivers his Lear with slick, almost playful efficiency, it is not his towering achievement. … Some of the dissonance is down to pace which, under Branagh’s direction, is as fast and feverish as Macbeth. So much takes place amid the shadows on Jon Bausor’s set design that it bears more than a few shades of that tragedy in its look... Staged at a hurtling two hours with no interval, it is

Branagh’s playful, furious, magnificent Lear is too big for this production … Our greatest living Shakespearean finally takes on Shakespeare's greatest role in a pared-down staging that doesn't quite do him justice … Of course our greatest living Shakespearian would take it upon himself to not only play but direct himself in Shakespeare’s greatest role sooner or later... Yet far from being the Kenneth Branagh show, this Lear, running at a scarcely believable two hours without interval, has the opposite problem: there is simply not enough of him. … Amid this slightly absurd neolithic pomp, Branagh’s hirsute Lear exerts dominion from the get go, radiating in those opening precipitous scenes a decidedly Trumpian impression of a ruler still very much calling the shots. Kenneth Branagh's radical, youthful Lear tugs at the soul … Though his take on 'the actor's Everest' initially fails to ignite, in the final third Branagh's performance is truly moving … His take on “the actor’s Everest … ... he’s cast it entirely from RADA graduates, mostly recent ones. Good on him for giving young actors a break in the West End, though it’s a bit old-school-tie to only support those from his own top-rank alma mater. … Peel away the brutal pruning of the text, and casting that is blind to age, ethnicity and gender, and this is a solidly old-fashioned staging. The verse-speaking is overly enunciated and emphatic. … What’s missing is a sense of conviction in the early stages of his performance that an external director might have identified and rectified. Kenneth Branagh’s show has glimpses of greatness … Here’s a Lear for the graphic novel era. Pace is everything in a production, directed by its star, Kenneth Branagh, that hurtles past in two hours without an interval. A monarch and his kingdom tumble into chaos in the blink of an eye. … Does all that energy add up to a dynamic, transcendent evening? Not exactly. If you had doubts about whether the actor-director has the gravitas to take on one of the great Shakespearean roles, you’d have them confirmed here. … Jessica Revell makes a winningly vulnerable Cordelia even if the decision to have her double as the Fool (as Michelle Terry did at the Globe last year) never quite convinces. … Jon Bausor’s set design is a distraction too. Kenneth Branagh’s bracingly idiosyncratic take on Shakespeare’s tragedy relocates the action to prehistoric times … Well, if we’re questioning the authenticity, it’s worth considering that Branagh’s production probably feels a lot closer to the England of circa 800 BC – when Shakespeare’s tragedy is nominally set – than the typical ‘Lear’. … There’s also little denying that our man looks good. You’d never believe he was 62, and while that might actually be a problem if he was your typical frail Lear, his interpretation of the role is as a powerful chieftain whose decision to give up his kingdom to his scheming daughters feels unusually reasonable. … So Branagh is good, and his take on King Lear as a character essentially ‘works’. Kenneth Branagh’s King Lear stars his favourite leading man: himself … Whoosh! The star is loud, clear and wraps up Shakespeare’s epic in two hours flat … He’s certainly full of beans as Shakespeare’s grim adventure begins. Don’t worry if you’ve got a cheap seat, Branagh speaks as if all his lines were written on the script in bold. … It all plays as the best rep production you’ve ever seen: a mighty exercise in rhythm and diction. … You wonder if Branagh the director is the best person to get the best from Branagh the actor. Yes, he’s been pulling off that double for 40 years, but there is a sweet spot to be found between pace and pathos with this approach, and he never really gives all this rage and ruin room to resonate.

Kenneth Branagh’s take on the thwarted ruler feels like a first draft … It’s the role that so many great Shakespearean actors hope to live up to, but Branagh’s West End performance of an ageing leader in decline feels like a curio rather than a complete reading … Generations of Shakespeare fans (and grumpy GCSE students) have grown up with Kenneth Branagh’s stylish, definitive film adaptations, including Henry V (1989), Othello (1995) and Hamlet (1996). So it’s unsurprising that there’s a cinematic, pared-down feel to his two-hour-long West End take on the role that so many great Shakespearean actors age into and hope to live up to: King Lear. … He sparks with energy as a warrior king who expects ritualistic pledges of allegiance from his daughters … This King Lear feels like a curio, one

Kenneth Branagh needs to stop directing himself … The entire thing has the feel of some dubious historical recreation for tourists … Kenneth Branagh may well be one of our finest stage actors – but he certainly isn’t one of the country’s leading theatre directors. Yet every time Branagh returns to the stage, he insists upon directing himself rather than entrusting the task to someone with an outside perspective. Kenneth Branagh's cut-back play leaves HIM looking like the fool … ... by choosing to direct himself in the title role of what's usually cited as Shakespeare's most challenging play (which opened in the West End last night), he has certainly fitted himself with a figurative jester's coxcomb. Even though the text has been slashed from three hours-plus to a wham-bam-thank-you-ma'am two hours (without interval), it's clear early on that we're in for a very long night. By hacking back the Bard's tale of an ancient Celtic monarch surrendering his kingdom to wicked daughters, he lays waste to the logic of chicanery and betrayals that lead Lear into madness and raging on a storm-blasted heath. … It's a performance of fearless virility, giving no clue as to why this hale and hearty monarch might w

Kenneth Branagh’s production is overblown and insubstantial … Kenneth Branagh’s take on Shakespeare’s tragedy is soulless … It’s perhaps Shakespeare’s most harrowing tragedy: an epic vortex of familial trauma, dementia, atrocity and war. Kenneth Branagh’s production – in which he also stars – fillets and compresses the play into just two interval-free hours. Yet it feels interminable. Confused in concept and clumsy in execution, it manages to be at once overblown and insubstantial. It is crammed with florid gesture and self-conscious declaiming, and offers scarcely a single moment of emotional truth. … At the centre – and giving a performance that feels weirdly detached from the actors around him... Kenneth Branagh savours Lear’s words rather too much … Howl. Kenneth Branagh’s rapid, over-elocuted King Lear has a shaggy vigour but misses the scope, the depth and – what is surely the play’s defining attribute – the terrifying dislocation of Shakespeare’s most far-ranging tragedy. Branagh directs and Branagh stars. Robustness is all. … Branagh, though he can make a line swing, delivers many of his speeches with peculiar consonantal explosiveness. He begins fuelled by anger, but with a twinkle, a touch of Father Christmas. As he unravels, he takes the roar down a notch, and unpicks his fluency … Above all, what is missing is the spread of sympathy that gives the play its reach. The poor naked wretches don’t get a look in here. This is less King Lear and more King Ken.
